questions.question: State the rules for direction and velocity ratio of meshed spur gears, the two properties of an idler, how ratios combine in a compound train with their effect on direction, and what bevel gears do, with a worked example of a 12-tooth driver at 1 200 revolutions per minute driving a 36-tooth gear.
questions.expected_answer: Two meshed spur gears always counter-rotate; the driver is turned by the effort and the driven gear is turned by it. Velocity ratio is driven teeth over driver teeth, equivalently driven over driver diameter, and driven speed is driver speed divided by the ratio: 36 over 12 gives 3, so the 36-tooth gear turns at 1 200 over 3, 400 revolutions per minute, slower and with three times the torque. An idler between two gears reverses direction a second time so the first and last gears turn the same way, and its size does not affect the ratio, which remains the last gear's teeth over the first gear's; idlers are made harder because each tooth meets two meshing points. In a compound train gears fixed on one shaft turn together and the ratios of the meshing pairs multiply, so two stages of 60 over 12 give 25, while each mesh reverses direction so two stages give the same output direction as the input and three stages the opposite. Bevel gears have teeth cut on cones and mesh with apexes meeting to turn the axis of rotation through 90 degrees under the same ratio rules, as in a hand drill, a speed increaser, or a car's axle, a reducer.

questions.question: Give the two formulas for mechanical advantage and when each applies, state the range of mechanical advantage for each class of lever with an example, explain gear mechanical advantage from teeth, and calculate the ideal effort for a crowbar with effort arm 1.5 metres and load arm 0.25 metres lifting 900 newtons, noting why the measured effort differs.
questions.expected_answer: For any machine, mechanical advantage is load divided by effort, both in newtons, with no unit; for a lever it also equals effort arm divided by load arm, both measured from the fulcrum in the same unit, without using moments. First-class levers with the fulcrum between effort and load, such as a crowbar or scissors, can have mechanical advantage above or below one; second-class levers with the load between fulcrum and effort, such as a wheelbarrow or bottle opener, always have mechanical advantage above one; third-class levers with the effort between fulcrum and load, such as a broom or the forearm, always have mechanical advantage below one and trade force for speed and distance. For gears, mechanical advantage equals the velocity ratio, driven teeth over driver teeth or driven over driver diameter, above one when a small gear drives a large one and below one when a large drives a small, multiplying through compound stages. The crowbar's mechanical advantage is 1.5 over 0.25, which is 6, so the ideal effort is 900 over 6, 150 newtons; the measured effort is somewhat higher because friction at the fulcrum and the weight of the bar absorb part of the effort, so the actual mechanical advantage is below the ideal.

questions.question: Summarise the conventions for drawing a gear system, a systems diagram and a working drawing, define the main steps of the design process as applied to the headgear project, and list the examination habits that save marks on this paper.
questions.expected_answer: A gear is drawn as its pitch circle with its tooth count beside it, a centre mark and a curved direction arrow; meshing circles touch at one point with centres apart by the sum of their pitch radii, driver and driven are labelled and the velocity ratio written. A systems diagram has input, process and output boxes joined by arrows carrying speeds, torques and directions, for example 400 revolutions per minute weak and clockwise in, 12T driving 48T at 4 to 1 with direction reversed, and 100 revolutions per minute with four times the torque anticlockwise out. A working drawing uses first-angle projection with the front view central, plan below and side view to the right, thick lines for visible edges, dashed for hidden detail and chain lines for centres, full-size dimensions in millimetres each given once, a parts list, and sloping members dimensioned by their ends. The design process: investigation with recorded sources; a brief stating problem, users, setting and purpose without the solution; measurable specifications with reasons and constraints as limits; two or more sketched ideas compared against the specifications; a working drawing before making; a budget of materials, labour, plant, fees, contingency and tax with sources; safe making to a planned sequence; evaluation testing each specification with numbers and recording failures with causes; and a presentation giving evidence. Habits: show ratio working for method marks, use units where they exist and none for ratios, draw with instruments when told to draw, flip direction at every mesh and say so, check which gear is the driver before dividing, answer written questions with a fact, a reason and an example, and leave no question blank.
